title: Probability Essentials
description: Reason clearly about chance, risk and evidence — the core tools behind statistics, games and decisions.
keyIdeas: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total **equally likely** outcomes.
'At least one' is easiest through the complement: **1 − P(none)**.
Conditional probability: shrink the world to what you know, then count.
Base rates matter: a positive test for a rare condition is often a false alarm.
Expected value = Σ value × probability — the long-run average.

concepts.label: Favourable over total
concepts.summary: With equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, a number from 0 to 1.

concepts.label: Equally likely outcomes
concepts.summary: Counting only works over outcomes that are equally likely, such as the 36 ordered pairs of two dice, not the 11 totals.

concepts.label: Independent events
concepts.summary: One event does not change the probability of the other, like repeated coin flips or drawing with replacement.

concepts.label: AND rule (multiply)
concepts.summary: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

concepts.label: OR rule (add)
concepts.summary: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); for mutually exclusive events the overlap is zero, so just add.

concepts.label: Complement trick
concepts.summary: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none): solve the easy opposite event instead of adding many cases.

concepts.label: Gambler's fallacy
concepts.summary: The false belief that after a streak the other outcome is "due", though independent trials have no memory.

concepts.label: Conditional probability
concepts.summary: P(A | B) is the probability of A given B: shrink the world to the cases where B is true, then count; P(A and B) ÷ P(B).

concepts.label: Base rate
concepts.summary: How common something is to begin with; with a rare condition most positive tests are false alarms. Count it with natural frequencies.

concepts.label: Flipping the condition
concepts.summary: P(A | B) is not P(B | A): P(positive | disease) differs from P(disease | positive).

concepts.label: Expected value
concepts.summary: EV = Σ value × probability: the average result per play over many repetitions; any single play can differ.

concepts.label: Multiplication principle
concepts.summary: If one choice has a options and another has b, together there are a × b possibilities.

concepts.label: Permutations
concepts.summary: Counting arrangements where order matters: n! ways to arrange n items, n × (n−1) × ... for the first k.

concepts.label: Combinations
concepts.summary: Counting selections where order does not matter: C(n, k) = n! ÷ (k! × (n−k)!), the ordered count divided by k!.

lessons.title: Counting outcomes
lessons.takeaway: Count equally likely outcomes: probability = favourable ÷ total.

steps.title: What probability is
steps.body:
**Probability** measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

When all outcomes are equally likely:

**P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes**

A fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes. Rolling an even number has 3 favourable outcomes (2, 4, 6), so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

steps.prompt: What's the probability of rolling a number **greater than 4** on a fair six-sided die?

steps.title: Two dice
steps.problem: You roll two fair dice. What's the probability the total is 7?
steps: List the possibilities: each die has 6 faces, so there are 6 × 6 = **36** equally likely ordered pairs.
steps.answer: P(total = 7) = 6/36 = **1/6** ≈ 0.167. It's the most likely total.

steps.prompt: Two fair dice: what is the probability the total is **8**? (decimal or fraction, e.g. 0.25 or 1/4)
steps.hint: List the pairs that add to 8, starting with (2,6).

steps.prompt: A classic mistake: *'There are 11 possible totals (2 to 12), so P(total = 2) = 1/11.'* What's wrong?
choices: The totals aren't equally likely — the 36 ordered pairs are
steps.explanation: The formula needs **equally likely** outcomes. A total of 2 needs (1,1) only: 1/36, while 7 has six ways.

steps.title: Roll two dice
steps.body:
Time to test the counting. Two dice have **36** equally likely ordered pairs, and **6** of them add up to 7, so P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%.

Roll a few times, then in hundreds. The dashed outlines are the exact shares from counting; the bars are what you actually rolled. Watch the bars grow into the triangle — and notice how rarely 2 or 12 turns up (1/36 each).

lessons.title: AND, OR, and the complement trick
lessons.takeaway: Independent AND → multiply; exclusive OR → add; 'at least one' → 1 − P(none).

steps.title: Combining events
steps.body:
Two events are **independent** if one doesn't affect the other (like two coin flips).

**AND (independent): multiply.** P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Two heads in a row: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

**OR (mutually exclusive): add.** If A and B can't both happen, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Rolling a 1 or a 2: 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3.

steps.prompt: Flip a fair coin 3 times. What's the probability of getting 3 heads?
You want P(card is a heart **or** a king) from a standard 52-card deck. Why can't you just add 13/52 + 4/52?
choices: The king of hearts would be counted twice
steps.explanation: When events overlap, subtract the overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = **16/52**.

steps.title: The complement trick
steps.body:
'At least one' questions have many cases to add up. Flip them around instead:

**P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)**

The complement, 'none', is usually a single AND, which is easy to multiply.

steps.title: At least one six
steps.problem: Roll a die 4 times. What's P(at least one six)?
steps: Each roll misses six with probability 5/6. The rolls are independent, so multiply: (5/6)⁴ = 625/1296 ≈ 0.482.
steps.answer: P(at least one six) ≈ **0.518** — slightly better than even odds.

steps.prompt: Flip a fair coin 5 times. What's the probability of **at least one** head?
steps.hint: First find P(no heads at all).

steps.prompt: A fair coin has landed tails 6 times in a row. What's the probability the next flip is heads?
choices: Less than 1/2 — tails is on a streak
steps.explanation: Flips are independent; the coin has no memory. Believing otherwise is the **gambler's fallacy**. (1/128 is the chance of the whole 7-flip sequence, calculated *before* any flips.)

steps.prompt: Does the result of the first step change the probabilities for the second? Sort each pair.

items.text: Flip a coin, then flip it again
Roll a die, then roll it again
Draw a card, put it back and shuffle, then draw again
Flip a coin and roll a die
Draw a card, keep it, then draw another
Take a sock out of a drawer, then take a second
Pick a class president, then a vice-president from the rest
Draw a raffle ticket, then draw a second without putting the first back

steps.hint: Does the first result change what's left to choose from? Putting the card back resets the deck.
steps.explanation: Coins, dice and a card that goes back into a shuffled deck have no memory: the second step has the same probabilities whatever happened first, so you can multiply straight away, e.g. 1/2 × 1/2 for two heads. Taking something out without putting it back changes what's left: after drawing an ace, only 3 of the 51 remaining cards are aces, so the chance of a second ace is 3/51 = 1/17, not 4/52 = 1/13. Socks, raffle tickets and a president who can't also be vice-president work the same way.

steps.title: Flip until it settles
steps.body:
Flip one at a time and you'll see streaks: three or four tails in a row is normal. Then flip by the thousand.

The share of heads drifts toward **50%**, but not because the coin makes up for a streak. Each flip is still 1/2. The early streaks just get **diluted** by thousands of new flips. This is the **law of large numbers**: the more trials, the closer the observed frequency tends to sit to the true probability.

lessons.title: Conditional probability and base rates
lessons.takeaway: Given B, shrink the world to B. For tests and evidence, count with natural frequencies and respect the base rate.

steps.title: Probability given information
steps.body:
**P(A | B)** means 'the probability of A, *given* that B happened'.

The idea: **shrink the world to the cases where B is true**, then ask how many of those also have A.

P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B)

steps.title: A die with a clue
steps.problem: You roll a fair die and someone tells you the result is even. What's the probability it's a 6?
steps: Shrink the world: the possible outcomes are now just {2, 4, 6} — 3 cases.
steps.answer: P(6 | even) = **1/3**, up from 1/6 without the clue.

steps.prompt: In a group of 40 people, 10 own a cat. Of the cat owners, 4 also own a dog. You pick a cat owner at random. What's the probability they own a dog?
steps.explanation: Restrict the world to the 10 cat owners: 4/10 = **0.4**. The other 30 people don't matter.

steps.title: Base rates
steps.body:
Conditional probabilities are easy to flip by mistake: P(positive test | disease) is **not** the same as P(disease | positive test).

The trick that makes this intuitive is **natural frequencies**: imagine 1,000 concrete people and count them.

steps.title: A medical test
steps.problem: A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it 90% of the time when it's present, but also gives a false positive for 9% of healthy people. You test positive. How likely is it that you have the disease?
steps: Imagine **1,000 people**. 1% → **10** have the disease, **990** don't.
Of the 10 sick people, 90% test positive → **9** true positives.
Of the 990 healthy people, 9% test positive → about **89** false positives.
Total positives ≈ 9 + 89 = 98. Only 9 of them are sick.
steps.answer: P(disease | positive) ≈ 9/98 ≈ **9%**. Most positives are false alarms because the disease is rare.

steps.prompt: Same test (detects 90%, 9% false positives), but now the disease affects **10%** of people. What's P(disease | positive)? Use 1,000 people. (decimal, e.g. 0.5)
steps.hint: 100 people are sick and 900 are healthy. How many of each group test positive?
steps.explanation: 100 sick → 90 positives. 900 healthy → 81 false positives. 90 / (90 + 81) = 90/171 ≈ **0.53**. A higher base rate makes a positive result far more meaningful.

steps.prompt: 5% of the parts a factory makes are defective. A scanner flags 80% of defective parts, but also 10% of good ones. A part gets flagged: how likely is it to be defective? Put the natural-frequency steps in order.
items: Split by the base rate: 50 defective, 950 good
Count the flagged ones in each group: 80% of 50 = 40, and 10% of 950 = 95
Shrink the world to the flagged parts: 40 + 95 = 135
steps.hint: Same recipe as the medical test: base rate first, then the test results inside each group.
steps.explanation: Start with a round crowd so every number is a count. The **base rate** splits it into 50 defective and 950 good parts. Then apply the scanner to each group: 40 true flags and 95 false ones. *Given* that a part is flagged, the world shrinks to those 135 parts, and only 40 of them are defective: 40/135 = 8/27 ≈ **0.30**. Even a decent scanner is wrong about most of its flags here, because good parts outnumber bad ones 19 to 1.

steps.prompt: *'Most car crashes happen within 5 miles of home, so driving far from home is safer.'* What's the flaw?
choices: It confuses P(near home | crash) with P(crash | near home) — most driving happens near home
5 miles is too short a distance to measure
steps.explanation: A high P(near home | crash) mostly reflects that most *driving* happens near home. The risk per mile could be the same or even lower.

lessons.title: Expected value
lessons.takeaway: EV = Σ value × probability. Use it to compare choices, remembering it's a long-run average.

steps.title: The long-run average
steps.body:
The **expected value** (EV) is the average result you'd get if you repeated something many times:

**EV = Σ (value × probability)**

A game: win $10 with probability 0.2, otherwise win $0. EV = 10 × 0.2 + 0 × 0.8 = **$2** per play.

steps.title: Is the bet worth it?
steps.problem: It costs $2 to play. You roll a die: on a 6 you get $10, otherwise nothing. Should you play?
steps: Roll a 6 → net +$8 (10 − 2), probability 1/6. Anything else → net −$2, probability 5/6.
steps.answer: EV ≈ **−$0.33** per play. On average you lose about 33 cents per game.

steps.prompt: A raffle ticket costs $5. There are 1,000 tickets and one prize of $2,000. What's the expected **net** value of buying one ticket?
steps.hint: Expected winnings first: prize × chance of winning. Then subtract the cost.
steps.explanation: Expected winnings: 2000 × 1/1000 = $2. Minus the $5 cost: EV = **−$3**.

steps.prompt: A bet has EV = +$1. What does that mean?
choices: Over many plays you gain about $1 per play on average — any single play can still lose
The chance of winning is above 50%
steps.explanation: EV is a **long-run average**. A bet can have positive EV and still lose most of the time (and vice versa).

steps.title: Why EV needs the long run
steps.body:
Back to the $2 game: a **6** pays $10. EV says you lose about **$0.33** per play, because you win 1/6 of the time: 10 × 1/6 − 2 ≈ −0.33.

Roll 10 times and your win rate could be anything — a lucky streak looks like a great bet. Keep rolling: the win rate settles near **1/6**, and the average result per play settles near the EV.

steps.prompt: Replacing your phone costs $600. There's a 5% chance per year you break it. Insurance costs $40/year. What's the expected yearly cost of **not** insuring?
steps.explanation: 600 × 0.05 = **$30** per year on average — less than the $40 premium. Insurance has negative EV on average; it's worth buying only when the loss would really hurt you.

lessons.title: Permutations and combinations
lessons.takeaway: Multiply independent choices; use n! for arrangements and C(n, k) when order doesn't matter.

steps.title: The multiplication principle
steps.body:
If one choice has *a* options and another has *b*, together there are **a × b** possibilities.

3 shirts × 4 trousers = 12 outfits.

steps.prompt: How many different 4-digit PINs are there (digits 0–9, repeats allowed)?

steps.title: Does order matter?
steps.body:
**Permutations** — order matters. Arranging *n* different items: n! = n × (n−1) × … × 1.

**Combinations** — order doesn't matter. Choosing k from n: C(n, k) = n! ÷ (k! × (n−k)!).

Picking a president *and* vice-president from 5 people: 5 × 4 = 20 (order matters). Picking a 2-person committee: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 (order doesn't).

steps.prompt: In how many different orders can you arrange 4 different books on a shelf?

steps.title: Choosing toppings
steps.problem: A pizza place offers 6 toppings. How many different 3-topping pizzas are possible?
steps: But each set of 3 toppings appears in 3! = 6 different orders, so we've counted each pizza 6 times.

steps.prompt: How many ways can you choose a 2-person team from 8 people?
steps.hint: Count ordered pairs, then fix the double counting.
steps.explanation: 8 × 7 = 56 ordered pairs; each team is counted twice → **28**.

steps.prompt: Does order matter? Sort each situation: count arrangements (permutations) or choices (combinations)?

items.text: Gold, silver and bronze for 3 of 10 runners
A president and a vice-president from a club of 12
A 5-card poker hand from a 52-card deck
Inviting 3 of your 10 friends to dinner

steps.hint: Swap two of the chosen items. If that gives a different outcome, order matters.
steps.explanation: **Order matters** when swapping gives something different: gold-silver isn't silver-gold (10 × 9 × 8 = 720 podiums), president-VP isn't VP-president (12 × 11 = 132), 4 guests fill 4 chairs in 4! = 24 ways. A 'combination' lock is a trap: 2-7-3 won't open a 3-7-2 lock, so order matters despite the name. **Order doesn't matter** when you only care *which* ones you picked: C(6, 3) = 20 pizzas, C(8, 2) = 28 teams, C(52, 5) = 2,598,960 hands, and C(10, 3) = 120 dinner groups, which is the 720 ordered picks divided by the 3! = 6 orders of each group.
